title: Hinweise zum Einsatz von künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) [Guidance on the use of artificial intelligence]
author: Frank Remmertz · Bundesrechtsanwaltskammer

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The guidance accepts the cluster’s emphasis on user competence and use-context-specific governance, and materially extends it by identifying an affirmative EU AI Act duty for providers and deployers to foster AI literacy. It adds concrete compliance factors—technical knowledge, experience, training, intended use and affected groups—plus the duty’s application timeline, without addressing the cluster’s broader empirical claims about productivity, verification or labour effects.
qs: 4 der KI-VO sind Anbieter und Betreiber von KI-Systemen verpflichtet, sicherzustellen, dass ihr Personal über ausreichende Kenntnisse und Kompetenzen im Umgang mit KI-Systemen 15 verfügt.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The guidance directly supports the cluster’s core copilot proposition: AI may assist but not replace lawyers, who retain personal responsibility and final control. Its categorical requirement to verify every AI result aligns especially with the cluster’s stricter view that verification burdens may limit efficiency, although it does not itself assess those efficiency costs.
qs: Daher sollte der Einsatz von KI-Systemen lediglich zur Unterstützung einer anwaltlichen Tätigkeit eingesetzt werden und darf diese nicht ersetzen.
In jedem Fall ist eine eigenverantwortliche Überprüfung und Endkontrolle der KI-Ergebnisse durch die Rechtsanwältin/den Rechtsanwalt erforderlich.

kp.k: Efficiency benefits coexist with persistent hallucination and bias risks
kp.d: The guidance describes AI as useful for analysis, document management, research and translation, and asserts efficiency benefits without quantifying them. Its focus is large language models: despite improvements since ChatGPT's November 2022 introduction, fabricated information and biased results remain risks requiring lawyer verification. It cites a Stanford University press release dated January 11, 2024, but reports no study sample or error rate.
qs: Anwendungen der künstlichen Intelligenz (KI) können auch in einer Anwaltskanzlei zur Effizienzgewinnung eingesetzt werden.

Seit der Einführung von „ChatGPT“ im November 2022 haben sich die Sprachmodelle zwar erheblich verbessert, Halluzinationen kommen aber immer noch vor und können im Einzelfall nicht ausgeschlossen werden.
Hinzu kommen Risiken verzerrter oder verfälschter Ergebnisse durch unzureichendes bzw. einseitiges Trainingsmaterial, was zusammenhängend unter dem Begriff „Bias“ bekannt ist.

kp.k: AI must support, not replace, personally accountable lawyers
kp.d: The guidance interprets technology-neutral BRAO and BORA duties, particularly conscientious practice under § 43 BRAO and personal performance under § 613 BGB, as requiring lawyers to retain independent responsibility. AI assistance does not transfer responsibility for advice or representation; lawyer verification and final review are required in every case.
qs: Die Vorschriften in der BRAO und der BORA sind technologieneutral, müssen also auch beachtet werden, wenn künstliche Intelligenz (KI) zum Einsatz kommt.
Daher sollte der Einsatz von KI-Systemen lediglich zur Unterstützung einer anwaltlichen Tätigkeit eingesetzt werden und darf diese nicht ersetzen.
In jedem Fall ist eine eigenverantwortliche Überprüfung und Endkontrolle der KI-Ergebnisse durch die Rechtsanwältin/den Rechtsanwalt erforderlich.

kp.k: Automation and client-facing uses increase required care
kp.d: The guidance states that duties of care rise with automation and intended use. Automated client communications, autoresponders and intake chatbots attract a higher standard than tools supporting internal workflows. Such systems must not suggest that individual lawyer review and advice are unnecessary.
qs: Die Sorgfaltsanforderungen im Umgang mit KI steigen mit dem Grad der Automatisierung und dem Einsatzzweck.
Es darf nicht der Eindruck entstehen, dass eine anwaltliche Prüfung und Beratung im Einzelfall nicht erforderlich sind.

kp.k: No general adoption duty, but operational exceptions exist
kp.d: As of December 2024, the guidance finds no general BRAO or BORA obligation to use AI, even where it would produce faster and more effective results for clients. However, the obligation to maintain necessary material, staffing and organisational resources under § 5 BORA may require legal-tech or AI tools in particular circumstances, such as mass proceedings. The document explicitly leaves future reassessment open.
qs: Es kann allerdings aufgrund der Kanzleipflicht nach § 5 BORA, die Rechtsanwältinnen und Rechtsanwälte verpflichtet, die für ihre jeweilige Berufsausübung erforderlichen sachlichen, personellen und organisatorischen Voraussetzungen vorzuhalten, im Einzelfall erforderlich sein, Legal-Tech- oder KI-Tools einzusetzen, bspw. zur Bearbeitung von Massenverfahren.

kp.k: Client confidentiality constrains prompts and document uploads
kp.d: Confidentiality under § 43a(2) BRAO covers all mandate information, including client names and the existence of the engagement, and continues after it ends. The guidance recommends abstract prompts that do not identify a matter even contextually and, where possible, fully anonymised uploads. Removing names and addresses alone may be insufficient; confidentiality breaches can also engage § 203 StGB.
qs: Wenn möglich, sollten bei Sprachmodellen nur „abstrakte“ Anfragen (sog. „prompts“) gestellt werden, die auch im Kontext keinerlei Rückschlüsse auf ein bestimmtes Mandat zulassen.
Soweit es erforderlich ist, Dokumente hochzuladen, sollten diese wenn möglich vorher vollständig anonymisiert sein.
Dabei reicht es regelmäßig nicht, Namen und Anschriften von Mandanten zu entfernen, wenn sich Mandatsinformationen aus dem Kontext ergeben können.

kp.k: Vendor access requires necessity and contractual confidentiality safeguards
kp.d: Under the guidance's interpretation of § 43e BRAO, AI vendors may receive confidential information only where necessary for the service. As of December 2024, it considers transmission of client secrets to models such as ChatGPT unnecessary, expressly qualifying this as applying at least to freely accessible operating models. Mere possible access counts, regardless of actual reading. Lawyers must carefully select providers and conclude contracts at least in text form containing statutory confidentiality, criminal-consequence notification and purpose-limitation provisions; cooperation must end immediately if safeguards cease to be assured.
qs: Danach dürfen Rechtsanwältinnen und Rechtsanwälte IT- Dienstleistern und damit auch Anbietern von KI-Lösungen nur dann Zugang zu vertraulichen Informationen gewähren, wenn dies für die Inanspruchnahme der Dienstleistung erforderlich ist.
Zu beachten ist hierbei auch, dass es für das Tatbestandsmerkmal des Zugangs zu Mandatsgeheimnissen nicht darauf ankommt, ob die KI-Anbieter tatsächlich Kenntnis nehmen.
Ist dies nicht (mehr) gewährleistet, muss die Zusammenarbeit gemäß § 43e Abs. 2 Satz 2 BRAO unverzüglich beendet werden.

kp.k: Cross-border outsourcing adds secrecy and data-protection requirements
kp.d: The guidance states that foreign providers must offer secrecy protection comparable to Germany's under § 43e(4) BRAO, alongside separate GDPR and BDSG compliance. It identifies uncertainty over whether data-protection standards establish comparable secrecy protection and recommends German or European server locations where possible. It calls for special safeguards in countries such as India or China. Its statement that OpenAI was absent from the relevant certified-company list is expressly dated December 2024, not presented as a timeless fact.
qs: Bei der Inanspruchnahme von KI-Lösungen aus dem Ausland muss der dort bestehende Geheimnisschutz nach § 43e Abs. 4 BRAO dem Schutz im Inland vergleichbar sein.

Zu beachten ist, dass neben den Anforderungen nach § 43e BRAO auch die Vorschriften zum Schutz personenbezogener Daten, insbesondere nach der DSGVO und dem BDSG, eingehalten werden müssen (§ 43e Abs. 8 BRAO).

kp.k: Client disclosure is recommended despite no general professional duty
kp.d: As of the guidance's date, the general duty to inform clients about material aspects of an engagement does not ordinarily establish a BRAO or BORA duty to disclose AI use. Contract law or unfair-competition law may nevertheless impose transparency obligations. The guidance recommends transparency and, where uncertain, contractual agreement with clients, while noting that professional-policy debate remains unsettled.
qs: Unabhängig davon ist ein transparenter Umgang mit KI-Tools und im Zweifel eine vertragliche Regelung mit den Mandanten empfehlenswert.
Die berufspolitische Diskussion dazu ist aber im Fluss, so dass empfohlen wird, die weiteren Entwicklungen aufmerksam zu verfolgen.

kp.k: AI literacy obligations require training and organisational preparation
kp.d: The guidance identifies lawyers and practice entities using AI under their own responsibility as generally being deployers under the EU AI Act. Article 4's AI-literacy requirement applies from 02.02.2025 and entails best-efforts measures sensitive to personnel knowledge, experience, training and use context. Staff instructions, training and understanding model operation and risks are central recommendations. Depending on firm size and extent of deployment, a risk-management system with documentation and monitoring duties may be necessary.
qs: Ganz wesentlich ist hierfür eine genaue Kenntnis der Funktionsweisen von KI-Tools und der damit verbundenen Risiken.

Im Einzelfall kann – abhängig von der Größe und dem Umfang des Einsatzes von KI-Systemen in einer Anwaltskanzlei – die Erstellung eines Risikomanagementsystems mit Dokumentations- und Überwachungspflichten erforderlich werden.
Zu beachten ist, dass diese Verpflichtung nach dem abgestuften zeitlichen Geltungsbereich der KI-VO in Art. 113 a) KI-VO bereits ab dem 02.02.2025 gilt.

kp.k: AI Act transparency distinguishes deployers from providers
kp.d: The guidance dates Article 50 transparency obligations to 02.08.2026. For law-firm deployers, disclosure of AI-generated public-interest texts may be relevant, although its application to lawyer publications is described as unclear; human review or editorial control coupled with editorial responsibility provides an exception. Providers have separate interaction-information and output-marking obligations, including for legal chatbots. Firms developing or commissioning systems under their own names can qualify as providers. Other EU or national transparency duties remain unaffected.
qs: Gemäß der KI-VO müssen Anbieter und Betreiber von KI-Systemen ab dem 02.08.2026 bestimmte Transparenzpflichten einhalten.
Die Pflichten sind für Anbieter und Betreiber jeweils unterschiedlich.
Damit besteht keine Offenlegungspflicht, wenn ein KI-generierter oder manipulierter Text von einer Rechtsanwältin bzw. Rechtsanwalt (oder Berufsausübungsgesellschaft) überprüft und verantwortet wird.

kp.k: Most law-firm tools are not currently considered high-risk
kp.d: The guidance provisionally considers most AI tools, including language models, outside the AI Act's high-risk category. It interprets Annex III point 8a's justice-related classification as addressing judicial authorities rather than lawyers. Individual systems can nevertheless qualify as high-risk on other grounds and attract additional duties. This assessment is qualified by pending developments, particularly expected Commission implementation guidelines.
qs: Abhängig vom jeweiligen KI-System im Einzelfall kann es sich um ein sog. Hochrisiko-KI-System handeln, wenngleich nach aktuellem Stand
Liegt ungeachtet dessen im Ausnahmefall ein Hochrisiko-KI-System vor, sind weitergehende Verpflichtungen nach der KI-VO zu beachten.

kp.k: AI Act compliance does not replace professional compliance
kp.d: The document treats the AI Act and lawyers' professional rules as parallel regimes. An AI Act-compliant system may still breach professional obligations, while violations of AI-literacy or transparency requirements can also have professional-law implications.
qs: Die Regelungen der KI-VO und die berufsrechtlichen Vorschriften stehen grundsätzlich nebeneinander.
Die Verwendung eines nach der KI-VO konformen KI-Systems kann gleichwohl gegen berufsrechtliche Vorschriften verstoßen.
Umgekehrt kann auch ein Verstoß gegen bestimmte Vorschriften der KI-VO wie Art. 4 KI-VO (KI-Kompetenz) oder Art. 50 KI-VO (Transparenzpflichten) berufsrechtlich relevant werden.

kp.k: Extensive automation raises copyright, tax and insurance risks
kp.d: The guidance warns that AI-generated text can infringe third-party copyright even though such text generally lacks copyright protection itself for want of personal intellectual creation. It also flags a conditional risk that sufficiently automated services may cease to qualify as legal professional activity and instead become commercial activity, with adverse tax consequences and possible denial of professional indemnity coverage. It specifies no automation threshold.
qs: Zusätzlich sind auch steuer- und versicherungsrechtliche Risiken zu beachten.
So kann ab einem gewissen Automatisierungsgrad fraglich sein, ob (noch) eine anwaltliche Tätigkeit vorliegt oder eine gewerbliche Tätigkeit mit negativen steuerlichen Folgen

kp.k: Guidance is provisional, advisory and requires case-specific judgment
kp.d: The document characterises itself as a non-exhaustive December 2024 snapshot, not a substitute for lawyers' independent assessment of permissible AI use in individual cases. It additionally recommends CCBE guidance and the European Bars Federation's 2023 guidance, while emphasising their advisory status. Rapidly developing professional-law debate warrants continued monitoring, and BRAK reserves the possibility of updating its guidance.
qs: Abschließend bleibt zu beachten, dass auch diese Orientierungshilfe nur empfehlenden Charakter hat und keinen Anspruch auf Vollständigkeit erhebt.

Sie dient als Hilfestellung bei dem verantwortungsbewussten Umgang mit KI-Tools, kann aber eine eigenverantwortliche Beurteilung der Zulässigkeit der Nutzung von KI-Anwendungen im Einzelfall nicht ersetzen.
Die BRAK behält sich vor, diese Hinweise zum geeigneten Zeitpunkt zu aktualisieren.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Remmertz presents AI as an efficiency-enhancing aid to German legal practice, not a replacement for lawyers’ personal responsibility, and identifies additional verification, confidentiality, competence and compliance burdens.
pts.d: In this BRAK guidance, Frank Remmertz states that AI brings noticeable efficiency gains through analysis, document management, research, translation and rapid text generation. Nevertheless, improved language models still produce hallucinations and biased results, requiring lawyers’ independent verification and final review. AI should support rather than replace legal work; greater automation and client-facing applications raise the required standard of care. There is generally no professional obligation to adopt AI, although the organisational requirements of particular practices, such as mass proceedings, may necessitate legal-tech or AI tools. Confidentiality restricts what lawyers may disclose to vendors: for language models such as ChatGPT, the guidance considers transmission of client secrets unnecessary at the then-current technical stage, at least for publicly accessible operating models. It recommends abstract prompts and, where possible, fully anonymised documents. AI adoption also entails staff competence measures and potentially risk management, documentation and monitoring. The guidance distinguishes the generally absent professional-law obligation to disclose AI use from possible contractual, unfair-competition and AI Act obligations. It also warns that generated text may infringe third-party copyright and that sufficiently automated services may raise questions about commercial tax treatment and professional indemnity coverage. These are operational and legal claims, not forecasts of employment losses, staffing restructuring or market shares.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source primarily supports its claims through legal interpretation and cited authorities, rather than quantified evidence of AI’s effects on legal services.
pts.d: The efficiency claim is not accompanied by productivity measurements, cost data or a described empirical study. For hallucination risk, Remmertz cites a Stanford University study through its January 11, 2024 press release, but reproduces no error rates or benchmark results. Bias is supported by a legal handbook citation. The requirements for personal responsibility and verification are grounded in § 43 BRAO and § 613 BGB; heightened care in client-facing automation is linked to OLG Hamm’s 'Scheidung Online' decision. Confidentiality and outsourcing analysis relies on §§ 43a and 43e BRAO, § 2 BORA, § 203 StGB, legal commentary and German data-protection guidance. Competence, transparency and high-risk classification claims derive from the EU AI Act. Tax and insurance risks are supported by secondary legal literature, not documented AI-related claims or losses. The patent decision cited alongside the copyright discussion serves as an analogy, not empirical evidence about generated legal texts. The guidance expressly describes itself as recommendatory and non-exhaustive.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims describe a December 2024 snapshot, with staged AI Act obligations from February 2025 and August 2026 and substantial qualifications based on deployment context.
pts.d: Remmertz expressly limits the absence of a general adoption obligation and the analysis of transmitting client secrets to the state of affairs in December 2024; the latter is qualified in a footnote as applying at least to publicly accessible operating models. The guidance acknowledges that professional-law positions may change. It says the AI Act’s AI-literacy obligation applies from February 2, 2025, while Article 50 transparency duties apply from August 2, 2026. Duties differ between deployers and providers. For public-interest text publication, it describes an exception to disclosure where human review or editorial control occurs and someone assumes editorial responsibility, while acknowledging uncertainty about the provision’s scope for lawyers’ publications. Most law-firm tools, including language models, are considered outside the high-risk category at the time of writing, but classification remains system-specific and subject to further developments and Commission guidance. Risk management may be needed depending on the scale and extent of AI use. Tax and insurance consequences are conditional risks at an unspecified degree of automation, not inevitable outcomes or dated predictions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are German lawyers and law firms, their staff and clients, with differentiated responsibilities for AI deployers and providers.
pts.d: Lawyers and professional practice entities receive potential efficiency benefits but retain independent responsibility for advice, representation and checking AI output. Practices handling mass proceedings are singled out as potentially needing technological tools to meet organisational requirements. Staff using AI are affected by competence and training measures. Clients may benefit from faster and more effective work but face risks from inaccurate advice, misleading automated interactions and disclosure of confidential information. Client-facing chatbots, automated communications and intake systems attract heightened care. AI vendors are subject to selection, contractual confidentiality and access restrictions when serving law firms. Larger professional practice entities may themselves qualify as AI providers if they develop or commission systems and deploy them under their own name or brand, with corresponding transparency obligations. Public readers may be affected by disclosure rules for AI-generated public-interest texts. The source does not claim different effects for law-firm staffing ranks, ALSPs, in-house legal departments or underserved access-to-justice populations.
